title: Read the odds, or learn them
hook: Would a rare loss matter equally after reading its odds and sampling outcomes?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Contrast described probabilities with experience that may omit rare outcomes.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Contrast described probabilities with experience that may omit rare outcomes.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy event has a 1% independent chance per draw. In twenty draws, about what is the chance you never see it? Toy inputs A=[0.01, 20]; B=[0.01, 200].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[81.79069375972307, 20, 1], [13.397967485796173, 200, 1]]. Labels: No rare event %, Draws, True rare %.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: A short experience can omit an outcome whose probability is explicitly known. The longer sample reduces that omission chance. A learner’s observed frequency and a described probability are different forms of evidence, especially for rare events.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Rare P=0.01, Draws=200. What is No rare event %? Answer: 13.398.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Rare P=0.01, Draws=200. What is No rare event %?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 13.398. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: Rare events are overweighted when described but underweighted when learned from experience (Hertwig, Barron, Weber & Erev, 2004).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Contrast described probabilities with experience that may omit rare outcomes.
